text: GDPR, CCPA, and HIPAA aren't governance laws, but every classification scheme, access control, and retention policy in a regulated organization traces back to one of them. This is an orientation overview, not legal advice. The goal is recognizing when a dataset might trigger one of these, so you know when to loop in the people who actually practice law.

GDPR took effect in 2018, and it protects the personal data of anyone in the EU, regardless of where the organization processing it is based. That extraterritorial scope is why a company with no EU office can still be subject to it. GDPR runs on an opt-in model: processing requires a documented legal basis before it happens, so the default is no. Violations carry fines up to twenty million euros or four percent of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

The California Consumer Privacy Act, expanded by the CPRA, gives California consumers the right to know what's been collected about them, to delete it, and to opt out of its sale or sharing. Unlike GDPR, CCPA runs on an opt-out model: collection is allowed by default, and the consumer has to take action to stop it. It's enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency.

That's the single clearest contrast between these two laws. GDPR is opt-in: the default is don't collect or use the data until there's a legal basis. CCPA is opt-out: the default is allowed, until the consumer says stop. Same goal, giving people control over their data, built on opposite defaults.

HIPAA, enacted in 1996, protects Protected Health Information held by covered entities, health plans, clearinghouses, and providers, and by their business associates. Three rules matter here: the Privacy Rule governs use and disclosure, the Security Rule sets safeguards specifically for electronic PHI, and the Breach Notification Rule requires telling affected individuals and HHS after a breach. HIPAA is enforced by the HHS Office for Civil Rights.
You don't need to practice law to do this work, just to recognize which law's category of data you're sitting on. Next up: SOX and the industry-specific rules that round out this regulatory picture.
